title: Shoulder Girdle & Shoulder Joint
summary: Covers the bones, joints and ligaments of the shoulder girdle and glenohumeral joint, scapular motions and the 2:1 scapulohumeral rhythm. Includes origin/insertion/action/innervation tables for shoulder girdle and shoulder joint muscles, end feel, and common shoulder pathologies such as AC separation, fractures, subluxation, impingement and frozen shoulder, plus a prime-mover review for the elbow, forearm and wrist.

sections.heading: The Shoulder Complex: Bones and Landmarks
body: The shoulder complex = shoulder girdle + shoulder (glenohumeral) joint. Its job is to place the hand in a huge variety of positions so it can perform tasks.
Bones: scapula, clavicle, humerus; the rib cage and sternum take part indirectly. The shoulder girdle itself is the scapula, clavicle and sternum.
Joints: sternoclavicular (SC), acromioclavicular (AC), glenohumeral (GH), and the scapulothoracic articulation (scapula gliding over the rib cage).

Scapula landmarks:
  • Superior angle - top of the vertebral border; attachment for levator scapulae.
  • Inferior angle - where vertebral and axillary borders meet; the reference point for judging scapular rotation (and a useful posture check).
  • Vertebral (medial) border - attachment of rhomboids and serratus anterior.
  • Axillary (lateral) border.
  • Spine - posterior ridge running from the medial border to the acromion; level with the T3-T4 spinous processes; attachment for middle and lower trapezius.
  • Acromion process - broad, flat superior-lateral tip; attachment for upper trapezius.
  • Coracoid process - anterior projection below the clavicle; attachment for pectoralis minor (also coracobrachialis and short head of biceps).
  • Glenoid fossa - shallow, slightly concave socket on the lateral side that articulates with the humeral head.
  • Subscapular, supraspinous and infraspinous fossae - origins of the rotator cuff muscles named for them.
Clavicle: sternal (medial) end and acromial (lateral) end. Sternum: manubrium (articulates with the clavicle), body, xiphoid process.

Humerus landmarks: head, anatomical neck, greater tubercle, lesser tubercle, intertubercular (bicipital) groove, deltoid tuberosity; distally the medial and lateral epicondyles, capitulum, trochlea and olecranon fossa.

sections.heading: Joints and Ligaments of the Shoulder Girdle
body:
Sternoclavicular (SC)Acromioclavicular (AC)
Articulating surfacesManubrium of sternum and sternal end of clavicleAcromion process of scapula and acromial end of clavicle
Joint typeSynovial; saddle (functions like ball-and-socket), triaxialSynovial; gliding (plane), biaxial
MotionClavicle moves on the stationary sternum: elevation/depression, protraction/retraction, anterior/posterior rotationAnterior/posterior and superior/inferior gliding, in step with SC and scapulothoracic motion
LigamentsSternoclavicular (anterior and posterior), costoclavicular, interclavicular, plus an articular discAcromioclavicular (superior, inferior), coracoclavicular (lateral/trapezoid and deep/conoid), coracoacromial

SC joint is the only direct attachment of the shoulder girdle (and upper limb) to the axial skeleton. Dislocation is rare because the disc and ligaments are so strong.
  • Anterior/posterior sternoclavicular ligaments limit anterior-posterior movement (each limits motion in the opposite direction).
  • Costoclavicular (clavicle to 1st rib) limits clavicular elevation.
  • Interclavicular (across the top of the manubrium, joining the two clavicles) limits clavicular depression.
  • Articular disc acts like a double hinge and absorbs shock, especially in a FOOSH (fall on outstretched hand).

AC joint ligaments:
  • Coracoclavicular suspends the scapula from the clavicle, limits scapular rotation and backward motion, and is the AC joint's main defense against shoulder separation.
  • Coracoacromial runs coracoid to acromion (both on the scapula, so it does not actually cross the AC joint) and forms the arch or roof over the humeral head, blocking upward dislocation.

Scapulothoracic articulation: the scapula gliding on the rib cage. It is not a true joint (no bony union or capsule) but provides motion and flexibility: elevation/depression, protraction/retraction, upward/downward and internal/external rotation, and anterior/posterior tilt.

sections.heading: Scapular Motions, Scapulohumeral Rhythm and Force Couples
body:
Scapular motions:
  • Elevation - shrug
  • Depression - lowering the shrug
  • Protraction (abduction) - reaching forward, as in a hug
  • Retraction (adduction) - squeezing the shoulder blades together
  • Upward rotation - inferior angle swings laterally/up as the arm is raised in flexion or abduction
  • Downward rotation - return to resting position as the arm is lowered
  • Scapular tilt - top of scapula tips forward when the shoulder hyperextends (swinging arms back)

Scapulohumeral rhythm: roughly the first 30 degrees of shoulder motion is mostly glenohumeral; after that, for every 2 degrees of shoulder motion the scapula rotates 1 degree (2:1 ratio). Example from class: at 60 degrees of flexion, (60 - 30) / 2 = 15 degrees of scapular rotation.

Clinical point: check scapular mobility before ranging a shoulder. If the scapula is tight, do not force the arm; mobilize and stretch the scapula first ("scap mobs"). The shoulder cannot move fully if the scapula does not move.

Shoulder joint motionAccompanying scapular motion
FlexionUpward rotation + protraction
ExtensionDownward rotation + retraction
HyperextensionScapular tilt
AbductionUpward rotation
AdductionDownward rotation
Internal (medial) rotationProtraction
External (lateral) rotationRetraction
Horizontal abductionRetraction
Horizontal adductionProtraction
Note that flexion and extension each pair with two scapular motions.

Force couple: muscles pulling in different directions that together produce one motion.
  • Upward rotation: upper trapezius (up), lower trapezius (down), serratus anterior (out/forward).
  • Downward rotation: pectoralis minor (down), rhomboids (in), levator scapulae (up).

Muscle reminders:
  • The direction of a muscle's fibers sets its line of pull and tells you how to stretch it (move opposite to every prime action).
  • Reversal of muscle action: the insertion becomes the stable end and the origin moves. Examples: pectoralis minor helps lift the ribs during forced breathing; trapezius helps lift the trunk in crutch walking.
  • Pectoralis minor is the only shoulder girdle muscle on the anterior surface of the body.
  • Weak or paralyzed serratus anterior (long thoracic nerve injury) causes scapular winging - the medial border lifts off the rib cage. Serratus anterior is also essential for full arm flexion.

Kinetic functional roles (Keough, Sain & Roller):
  • Scapular pivoters - trapezius, serratus anterior, levator scapulae, rhomboids (move the scapula on the thorax).
  • Humeral positioners - anterior, middle, posterior deltoid.
  • Humeral propellers - latissimus dorsi, pectoralis major, teres major.
  • Shoulder protectors - rotator cuff, which force-couples with the deltoid to keep the joint safe.

sections.heading: The Glenohumeral Joint: Structure and Motions
body: The glenohumeral (shoulder) joint is a synovial ball-and-socket (triaxial) joint between the humeral head and the glenoid fossa. It moves in all three planes around all three axes - one of the most mobile and least stable joints in the body.

MotionPlaneAxisNormal ROMEveryday example
FlexionSagittalFrontal0-180Raising hands overhead
ExtensionSagittalFrontal180-0Bringing a cup down from a cupboard
HyperextensionSagittalFrontal0-60Bowling backswing
AbductionFrontalSagittal0-180Arms up in a jumping jack
AdductionFrontalSagittal180-0Arms down in a jumping jack
Medial (internal) rotationTransverseVertical0-70Reaching for a seatbelt
Lateral (external) rotationTransverseVertical0-90Tennis forehand swing
Horizontal abductionTransverseVertical0-40 (from 90 abd)Opening arms for a hug
Horizontal adductionTransverseVertical0-130 (from 90 abd)Hugging yourself
Scaption is elevation in the scapular plane, about 30 degrees forward of the frontal plane - most functional reaching happens here. Circumduction combines flexion, abduction, extension and adduction.

Full abduction (and full flexion) requires external rotation so the greater tubercle clears the acromion instead of jamming under it. The rotator cuff must work with the deltoid so the humeral head rolls and glides down while the arm rises.
Some muscles must co-contract to cancel unwanted actions: e.g., the anterior deltoid flexes and horizontally adducts, so to get pure flexion another muscle must counter the horizontal adduction.

sections.heading: Glenohumeral Ligaments, Supporting Structures and End Feel
body:
• Joint capsule - attaches around the glenoid rim and the anatomical neck of the humerus; outer fibrous and inner synovial layer; creates a vacuum that helps hold the humeral head in the fossa. A tear in the capsule or labrum loses this vacuum.
  • Glenoid labrum - fibrocartilage rim that deepens the shallow glenoid fossa, increasing contact and stability; often damaged in dislocation.
  • Glenohumeral ligaments (superior, middle, inferior) - folds of the capsule that reinforce its anterior side.
  • Coracohumeral ligament - supports the superior joint (part of the roof).
  • Coracoclavicular ligament - keeps the AC joint from separating.
  • Subacromial space - narrow gap between the humeral head and the underside of the acromion; contains the subdeltoid/subacromial bursa, the supraspinatus and infraspinatus tendons and the long head of biceps.
  • Bursae - fluid-filled sacs that reduce friction between tissues; vulnerable to compression with repetitive overhead motion (bursitis = inflammation of a bursa).
  • Rotator cuff (SITS) - Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor, Subscapularis; keep the humeral head centered and rotating in the glenoid fossa.

End feel is what the examiner feels at the end of passive ROM:
  • Bony/hard - abrupt bone-on-bone stop (elbow or knee extension).
  • Soft tissue stretch/firm - firm with slight give from ligaments, capsule and muscle (shoulder motions, e.g. flexion).
  • Soft tissue approximation/soft - muscle bulk or fat meets (elbow flexion).
  • Abnormal - an end feel that occurs where it should not, or at the wrong point in the range.

Stretching a muscle = move the joint opposite to every prime action (e.g., stretch latissimus dorsi with flexion, abduction and external rotation; stretch subscapularis with external rotation). The same opposite motions give the direction of resistance when strengthening.

Concentric vs eccentric: concentric strengthening resists the muscle while it shortens through its prime action; eccentric strengthening controls the motion as the muscle lengthens (e.g., slowly lowering the arm from abduction works the middle deltoid and supraspinatus eccentrically).

sections.heading: Common Shoulder Pathologies
body:
AC separation (separated shoulder):
  • 1st degree - AC ligament stretched.
  • 2nd degree - AC ligament ruptured, CC ligament stretched.
  • 3rd degree - AC and CC ligaments both ruptured.
Clavicle fracture - the most frequently broken bone in children; usually from a FOOSH or a fall onto the lateral shoulder.

Humeral fractures - rising with an aging population, sports and osteoporosis.
  • Humeral (surgical) neck fracture - common in the elderly; often an impacted fracture.
  • Mid-humeral (shaft) fracture - direct blow or twisting force, often spiral; about 18% injure the radial nerve as it wraps the shaft, causing weak wrist extension (wrist drop) and lost sensation on the dorsum of the hand. Most recover in 3-4 months.
  • Supracondylar (distal) fracture - an elbow fracture that can damage muscles, nerves and vessels; risk of compartment swelling and Volkmann's (ischemic) contracture. Treated with closed reduction or ORIF, 4-6 weeks casting, then splinting. Therapy: ROM, strength, endurance; avoid prolonged dependent positioning and watch the pain cycle (risk of CRPS).
  • Pathological fracture - from weakened bone: osteoporosis, tumors, metastatic cancer.
Anterior shoulder dislocation - forced abduction with external rotation drives the humeral head anteriorly out of the glenoid; the labrum is often damaged.

Glenohumeral subluxation - common after CVA or TBI when paralyzed muscles (especially the rotator cuff and deltoid) can no longer hold the humeral head in the fossa. The subluxation itself is not painful; pain comes from mishandling it (e.g., pulling on the arm or forcing ROM causes impingement).

Impingement syndrome - overuse pinching of soft tissue (rotator cuff, bursa, long head of biceps) between the humeral head and the coracoacromial arch; "swimmer's shoulder" (freestyle, butterfly, backstroke).

Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) - capsule thickens and tightens, causing pain and loss of ROM. Most common in women over 40 and in people with diabetes, cervical disc disease or post-stroke hemiplegia. Stages: (1) freezing/painful, 2-9 months, progressive pain worse at night; (2) frozen/stiffening, 4-12 months, lost ROM and ADL use with dull ache; (3) thawing, 5-24 months, ROM and function return.
Rotator cuff tendonitis/tear - acute trauma or gradual degeneration of the SITS tendons (supraspinatus most often).
Bicipital tendonitis - the long head of biceps tendon rubs as it crosses the humeral head in its groove, often with rotator cuff weakness; inflamed by repetitive motion.
Erb's palsy - upper brachial plexus (C5-C6) injury, usually in newborns after a difficult delivery; weakness or paralysis of the arm.

body: From the upper extremity prime-mover answer chart (Girdle, Shoulder, Elbow, Forearm, Wrist):

RegionMotionPrime movers
ElbowFlexionBrachialis, brachioradialis, biceps brachii (pronator teres assists)
ElbowExtensionTriceps brachii, anconeus
ForearmSupinationSupinator, biceps brachii
ForearmPronationPronator teres, pronator quadratus
WristFlexionFlexor carpi ulnaris, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus
WristExtensionExtensor carpi ulnaris, extensor carpi radialis longus, extensor carpi radialis brevis

All of these wrist muscles cross the elbow, so they assist elbow flexion. Keep the elbow extended when stretching any of them.

terms.def: Shoulder girdle plus glenohumeral joint working together to position the hand.
Scapula, clavicle and sternum, linked by the SC and AC joints.
Top corner of the scapula's vertebral border; attachment for levator scapulae.
Lowest point of the scapula where the vertebral and axillary borders meet; reference for scapular rotation.
Medial border of the scapula; attachment for rhomboids and serratus anterior.
Posterior ridge from the medial border to the acromion, level with T3-T4; attachment for middle and lower trapezius.
Flat superior-lateral tip of the scapula that articulates with the clavicle; attachment for upper trapezius.
Anterior hook-like projection of the scapula; attachment for pectoralis minor, coracobrachialis and short head of biceps.
Shallow socket on the lateral scapula that receives the humeral head.
Lateral bump on the proximal humerus; insertion of supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor.
Anterior bump on the proximal humerus; insertion of subscapularis.
Groove between the tubercles holding the long head of biceps tendon; site of pec major, lat and teres major insertions.
Roughened area on the lateral humeral shaft where the deltoid inserts.
Synovial saddle joint (triaxial) between the manubrium and the clavicle; the only direct attachment of the upper limb to the axial skeleton.
Synovial gliding (biaxial) joint between the acromion and the lateral clavicle.
Fibrocartilage disc in the SC joint that acts as a double hinge and absorbs shock.
Connects the clavicle to the first rib; limits clavicular elevation.
Joins the two clavicles across the manubrium; limits clavicular depression.
Suspends the scapula from the clavicle and prevents AC separation.
Runs coracoid to acromion forming the roof over the humeral head; prevents upward dislocation.
Scapula gliding over the rib cage; functional but not a true joint.
Fall On OutStretched Hand; common cause of clavicle and other UE fractures.
Scapula moves away from the spine (forward reach, hug).
Scapula moves toward the spine (squeezing shoulder blades).
Inferior angle rotates laterally and up as the arm is raised.
Top of the scapula tips forward, accompanying shoulder hyperextension.
After the first ~30 degrees, a 2:1 ratio of glenohumeral to scapular motion during arm elevation.
Muscles pulling in different directions that together produce one motion.
The insertion becomes stable and the origin moves (e.g., pec minor lifting ribs).
Medial border of the scapula lifts off the thorax, usually from serratus anterior weakness (long thoracic nerve).
Trapezius, serratus anterior, levator scapulae and rhomboids, which move the scapula on the thorax.
Latissimus dorsi, pectoralis major and teres major, which drive the humerus powerfully.
Synovial ball-and-socket (triaxial) joint between the humeral head and glenoid fossa; highly mobile, less stable.
Arm elevation in the scapular plane, about 30 degrees anterior to the frontal plane.
Circular combination of flexion, abduction, extension and adduction.
Fibrocartilage rim deepening the glenoid fossa for stability.
Fibrous/synovial sleeve from the glenoid rim to the anatomical neck that creates a stabilizing vacuum.
Ligament supporting the superior side of the GH joint.
Gap under the acromion containing the bursa, supraspinatus/infraspinatus tendons and long head of biceps.
Fluid-filled sac that reduces friction between tissues; inflammation is bursitis.
Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis; keep the humeral head centered in the glenoid.
The quality of resistance felt at the end of passive ROM.
Firm stop with slight give from capsule/ligament/muscle tension; normal for the shoulder.
Muscle shortens while producing force.
Muscle lengthens under control while producing force.
Sprain of the AC (and possibly CC) ligaments, graded 1st-3rd degree.
Overuse pinching of rotator cuff, bursa or biceps tendon under the coracoacromial arch.
Frozen shoulder: thickened, tight capsule causing pain and lost ROM in three stages.
Partial downward displacement of the humeral head, common after stroke.
Ischemic deformity of the forearm after supracondylar fracture with compartment swelling.
Upper brachial plexus birth injury causing arm weakness/paralysis.
Complex Regional Pain Syndrome; a risk when pain, swelling and dependent positioning persist after injury.

questions.q: Which joint is the only direct bony attachment of the shoulder girdle to the axial skeleton?
questions.explain: The SC joint links the clavicle to the manubrium, the trunk's only direct connection to the upper limb.

questions.q: Which bones make up the shoulder girdle?
questions.explain: The shoulder girdle is the scapula, clavicle and sternum; the humerus belongs to the shoulder joint.

questions.q: Which scapular landmark is used as the reference point for judging upward and downward rotation?
questions.explain: Rotation is described by which way the inferior angle moves.

questions.q: Pectoralis minor attaches to which scapular landmark?
questions.explain: Pec minor runs from ribs 3-5 to the coracoid process.

questions.q: What type of joint is the acromioclavicular joint?
questions.explain: The AC joint is a plane/gliding joint allowing two directions of glide.

questions.q: Which ligament limits elevation of the clavicle at the SC joint?
questions.explain: The costoclavicular ligament ties the clavicle down to the first rib.

questions.q: Which ligament limits clavicular depression?
questions.explain: The interclavicular ligament across the manubrium stops the clavicle dropping.

questions.q: Why is dislocation of the SC joint rare?
choices: It is a fibrous joint with no motion
Its articular disc and ligaments are very strong
questions.explain: The disc and strong ligaments make the SC joint very stable.

questions.q: Which structure forms the arch or roof over the humeral head and blocks upward dislocation?
questions.explain: The coracoacromial ligament spans coracoid to acromion above the humeral head.

questions.q: Which ligament suspends the scapula from the clavicle and is key to preventing shoulder separation?
questions.explain: The coracoclavicular ligament holds the scapula to the clavicle.

questions.q: Why is the scapulothoracic articulation called an atypical or 'not true' joint?
choices: There is no direct bony union or capsule; the scapula glides on muscle over the ribs
questions.explain: The scapula moves over the thorax without a true articular connection.

questions.q: A client shrugs their shoulders toward their ears. Which scapular motion is this?
questions.explain: A shrug is scapular elevation.

questions.q: Reaching forward to push a door open mainly involves which scapular motion?
questions.explain: Protraction slides the scapula forward around the thorax.

questions.q: Using scapulohumeral rhythm, about how much scapular rotation accompanies 90 degrees of shoulder flexion?
questions.explain: (90 - 30) / 2 = 30 degrees of scapular rotation.

questions.q: After the first ~30 degrees of elevation, the glenohumeral-to-scapular motion ratio is:
questions.explain: Two degrees of shoulder motion for every one of scapular rotation.

questions.q: Before performing PROM on a client's shoulder, the OTA notes the scapula is very tight. What should be done?
choices: Force the shoulder through full range anyway
Mobilize and stretch the scapula before ranging the shoulder
questions.explain: The shoulder cannot move fully without scapular motion, so mobilize the scapula first.

questions.q: Shoulder flexion is accompanied by which scapular motions?
questions.explain: Flexion pairs with upward rotation plus protraction.

questions.q: Shoulder hyperextension is accompanied by which scapular motion?
questions.explain: The scapula tilts when the arm swings back behind the body.

questions.q: External rotation of the shoulder is accompanied by which scapular motion?
questions.explain: Lateral rotation pairs with scapular retraction.

questions.q: Which group of muscles forms the force couple for scapular upward rotation?
choices: Upper trapezius, lower trapezius, serratus anterior
Latissimus dorsi, teres major, pectoralis major
questions.explain: These three pull in different directions to rotate the scapula upward.

questions.q: Which muscle is NOT part of the downward-rotation force couple?
questions.explain: Serratus anterior is an upward rotator.

questions.q: What nerve innervates the trapezius?
questions.explain: The trapezius is supplied by cranial nerve XI.

questions.q: The rhomboids and levator scapulae share which nerve?
questions.explain: Both are innervated by the dorsal scapular nerve.

questions.q: Injury to the long thoracic nerve causes scapular winging because it supplies which muscle?
questions.explain: Serratus anterior holds the medial border against the thorax.

questions.q: Which part of the trapezius is a prime mover for scapular retraction only?
questions.explain: Middle trapezius fibers run horizontally and pull the scapula toward the spine.

questions.q: To stretch the levator scapulae, the scapula should be moved into:
questions.explain: Stretch by moving opposite to its elevation and downward rotation.

questions.q: Which shoulder girdle muscle lies on the anterior surface of the body?
questions.explain: Pec minor is the only anterior shoulder girdle muscle.

questions.q: A client on crutches lifts their trunk by pushing down through the arms. This is an example of:
questions.explain: The origin moves toward the stable insertion, lifting the trunk.

questions.q: Which muscles are classified as humeral propellers?
choices: Latissimus dorsi, pectoralis major, teres major
questions.explain: The propellers are the large muscles that drive the humerus.

questions.q: In which plane and around which axis does shoulder abduction occur?
questions.explain: Abduction moves sideways in the frontal plane around a front-to-back axis.

questions.q: What is the normal ROM for shoulder lateral (external) rotation?
questions.explain: Lateral rotation is about 90 degrees; medial rotation is about 70.

questions.q: Normal shoulder hyperextension ROM is approximately:
questions.explain: Hyperextension reaches about 60 degrees.

questions.q: Why must the humerus externally rotate to achieve full abduction?
choices: So the greater tubercle clears the acromion instead of impinging under it
questions.explain: External rotation turns the greater tubercle away from the acromial arch.

questions.q: Scaption occurs in which plane?
choices: The scapular plane, about 30 degrees anterior to the frontal plane
questions.explain: Scaption is elevation in the plane of the scapula, where most functional reaching occurs.

questions.q: Which describes the glenohumeral joint?
choices: Synovial ball-and-socket, triaxial, very mobile but less stable
questions.explain: The GH joint trades stability for mobility in all three planes.

questions.q: Which structure deepens the glenoid fossa to increase stability?
questions.explain: The labrum is a fibrocartilage rim around the glenoid.

questions.q: What is the normal end feel of the shoulder joint?
questions.explain: Shoulder motions stop with firm capsular/ligament tension.

questions.q: Which muscle is NOT part of the rotator cuff?
questions.explain: SITS: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis.

questions.q: Which structures lie in the subacromial space?
choices: Articular disc of the SC joint
Subdeltoid bursa, supraspinatus and infraspinatus tendons, long head of biceps
questions.explain: These tissues are compressed in impingement.

questions.q: How does the GH joint capsule help hold the humeral head in place?
choices: It is fused to the labrum with bone
questions.explain: The sealed capsule's negative pressure helps keep the head seated.

questions.q: What is the nerve supply of the deltoid?
questions.explain: All three deltoid heads are supplied by the axillary nerve.

questions.q: Which rotator cuff muscle inserts on the lesser tubercle and internally rotates the shoulder?
questions.explain: Subscapularis is the only cuff muscle on the lesser tubercle.

questions.q: Which muscle initiates shoulder abduction and lies under the acromion?
questions.explain: Supraspinatus starts abduction and is most often torn.

questions.q: Infraspinatus and teres minor both perform which actions?
questions.explain: Both insert on the greater tubercle posteriorly and laterally rotate.

questions.q: To stretch the latissimus dorsi, move the shoulder into:
questions.explain: Stretch by reversing its extension, adduction and internal rotation.

questions.q: Which nerve supplies the latissimus dorsi?
questions.explain: The thoracodorsal nerve innervates the lat.

questions.q: Which deltoid head is the prime mover for horizontal abduction and hyperextension?
questions.explain: Posterior fibers from the scapular spine pull the arm back.

questions.q: A client slowly lowers their arm from 90 degrees of abduction to their side. The middle deltoid is working:
questions.explain: The deltoid lengthens under control as the arm lowers against gravity.

questions.q: In a 3rd degree AC separation:
choices: Only the AC ligament is stretched
Both AC and CC ligaments are ruptured
questions.explain: Third degree means both ligament groups are torn.

questions.q: Which is the most frequently broken bone in children?
questions.explain: Clavicle fractures commonly result from FOOSH or falls on the shoulder.

questions.q: A client with a spiral mid-shaft humeral fracture now has weak wrist extension and numbness on the back of the hand. Which nerve is likely involved?
questions.explain: The radial nerve wraps the humeral shaft in the spiral groove.

questions.q: Which mechanism typically causes an anterior shoulder dislocation?
questions.explain: Abduction plus ER levers the humeral head anteriorly.

questions.q: A client after a stroke has a subluxed shoulder. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The subluxation itself is not painful, but improper handling can cause impingement and pain
The arm should be pulled to assist transfers
Full aggressive ROM will reduce it
questions.explain: Pain comes from mishandling, so protect and position the arm.

questions.q: During which stage of adhesive capsulitis does ROM begin to return?
questions.explain: The thawing stage brings back ROM and function.

questions.q: Impingement syndrome ('swimmer's shoulder') involves compression of soft tissues between the humeral head and the:
questions.explain: Repetitive overhead motion pinches the cuff and bursa under the arch.

questions.q: Volkmann's contracture is a risk after which fracture?
questions.explain: Swelling in the forearm compartment after distal humeral fracture causes ischemia.

questions.q: Erb's palsy is most often caused by:
choices: Brachial plexus injury during a difficult birth
questions.explain: Stretch of the upper brachial plexus at delivery leads to arm weakness.

questions.q: Which muscles are prime movers of forearm supination?
questions.explain: Supinator and biceps turn the palm up.

questions.q: Which wrist muscle produces both extension and ulnar deviation?
questions.explain: ECU extends and ulnarly deviates the wrist.

questions.q: Why should the elbow be kept extended when stretching the wrist flexors and extensors?
choices: It protects the radial nerve from compression
These muscles cross the elbow, so elbow extension lengthens them fully
questions.explain: Their origins at the epicondyles mean they assist elbow flexion.
